deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler models wall friction in a moving liquid as a force proportional to the local pressure, not to velocity. In modern terms this is a Coulomb-type law. The pressure p is measured as a head and includes the atmospheric head l (about 30 ft of water). On a slice of a tube of cross-section gg, the friction term is (α/g)·p·dz. Integrating the steady momentum balance down a vertical outlet tube BC of length b, attached to a vessel AB with water depth a, gives exponentials e^{±αb/g}. The outlet orifice has area kk.

Previous page: Euler requires the pressure to stay positive everywhere, otherwise the water leaves the wall. To first order in α he found the pressure at BB to be R = l + a − (k^4/g^4)(a+b). For an open tube this forces b < l. With b = l he gets the efflux head v = a + l − αl²/(2g).

§54: If the vessel term a/f is negligible against b/g, then 𝔄 = 1 and A = a/f. This gives
v = [a e^{−αb/g} + (g/α)(1−e^{−αb/g}) − l(1−e^{−αb/g})] / [1 − (k^4/g^4)(1−e^{−αb/g})].
For a fully open tube (k = g) the denominator becomes e^{−αb/g}, and
v = a + (g/α − l)(e^{αb/g} − 1).

§55: Because of the factor (g/α − l), the critical width is g = αl. At that width v = a exactly, independent of b: the tube adds no speed over efflux at BB with no tube. For narrower tubes the friction loss outweighs the gain from the added fall. With g = αl/2 one gets v = a − (l/2)(e^{2b/l} − 1), which is about a − b − b²/l for b ≪ l. Hence no flow unless a > b (to leading order).

§56: Generally, with g = αl/n, v = a − ((n−1)/n)·l·(e^{nb/l} − 1), which is about a − (n−1)b. A fine enough ('capillary') tube can therefore stop efflux entirely. This yields an experiment to measure α. Shorten the tube until flow just starts, or (§57) raise the head a until flow just starts. Then a = (n−1)b, so n = (a+b)/b and α = ((a+b)/b)·(g/l).

The page thus serves the program of E260: deriving observable consequences, and a measurement scheme for α, from a pressure-proportional friction law in pipe flow.
errors: v = a − ((n−1)/n)l(e^{nb/l}−1) = a − (n−1)b is written as an equality, but it is only first order in nb/l. Since n = (a+b)/b, it needs a+b ≪ l. The exact threshold is e^{nb/l} − 1 = na/((n−1)l), not n = (a+b)/b.
'nisi sit a > b + bb/l, hoc est nisi sit a > b' silently drops the second-order term. This is acceptable only to leading order.

Physical gap: the friction law (proportional to pressure, independent of velocity) is wrong for water. Viscous resistance depends on velocity (Hagen 1839, Poiseuille 1840). The predicted complete arrest of flow is a static-friction / yield-stress artefact.

Physical gap in the proposed experiments (§§56–59): for tubes of diameter about a line, capillarity (surface tension, Jurin's law) dominates and does hold water in vertical tubes. Euler ignores it, so the experiment would measure capillary retention, not α.

ideas.what: Wall friction proportional to local pressure, giving a linear first-order ODE for pressure along a vertical tube with exponential solutions
ideas.modern_name: Coulomb (pressure-proportional) wall friction; mathematically the same form as the Janssen silo equation dp/dz = ρg − (4μK/D)p
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler for the hydraulic version (E260); Janssen 1895 for granular silos
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Comm. Petrop. 6 (1756/57, publ. 1761); discussed by Truesdell in Opera omnia II.12 introduction (unsure of detail)

ideas.what: Critical tube width g = αl, at which the attached tube neither speeds up nor slows down efflux, with total arrest for narrower tubes
ideas.modern_name: Yield/threshold condition for flow under Coulomb-type friction (analogous to Bingham yield stress or plug flow arrest)

ideas.what: Measuring the friction coefficient from the onset of flow in a capillary (varying length or head)
ideas.modern_name: Threshold (onset-of-flow) measurement of a friction coefficient

ideas.what: First-order expansion of exponentials to get v ≈ a − b − b²/l and v ≈ a − (n−1)b

missed.claim: Euler's pressure-proportional wall-friction model gives exactly the exponential pressure profile later known as Janssen's law for silos (1895). Its consequence is that a narrow enough tube can arrest flow regardless of length. Euler's 'α' plays the role of Janssen's μK, and g plays the role of the hydraulic radius. The mathematics and the threshold/arrest phenomenon fit granular or frictional media, not water.
missed.quote: Tubus igitur BC tam gracilis esse potest, vt frictio effluxum aquae per eius orificium CC penitus arceat
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical precursor of the Janssen effect and of granular discharge arrest (clogging/yield) in vertical channels. Histories of granular mechanics start with Janssen and Coulomb, apparently without noting E260. It is a minor historiographical link.

missed.claim: Euler proposes a capillary experiment whose real outcome (water retained in thin vertical tubes, §59) would occur through surface tension, not friction. This makes it a rare case of an 18th-century friction theory that would be falsely 'confirmed' by capillarity.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of historical interest only, for the reception of E260's friction law.

deep.surprise_reason: The computations are correct to first order and are routine given Euler's (physically wrong) friction law. The only possibly underappreciated point is that the model is mathematically the Janssen granular-friction equation, with a flow-arrest threshold. That is a modest historiographical connection, not a hidden result.
transcription_corrections: The transcription of this page matches the image well; the formulas in §§54–56 are correct as transcribed.
